scenes.title: Where Demand Meets Supply
scenes.summary: Touch why a liter of gasoline costs what it costs. Quantity demanded Q_d = a - bP falls as price rises; quantity supplied Q_s = dP rises. The point where the two match — Q_d = Q_s — is the equilibrium.

scenes.title: Splitting the Lunch Budget
scenes.summary: Split a 40 lunch budget between two foods. The money constraint is one line: p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = m. The best combo is where the last won buys the same happiness everywhere — raise a price and watch that point slide.

scenes.title: The Cafe Owner's Math
scenes.summary: You run a cafe. The cost of one more cup is MC = \Delta C / \Delta q — rising with every cup. While the price P beats that cost, selling pays; stopping at P = MC is the answer.

scenes.title: Competition vs Monopoly
scenes.summary: The same streaming market, side by side: competition left, monopoly right. The monopolist stops at MR = MC, and the lost triangle (deadweight loss) glows red. Lower the demand responsiveness and the red triangle grows — insensitive customers hurt more.

scenes.title: Taxes and Price Ceilings
scenes.summary: Who pays a 3 cigarette tax? The tax wedge P_b = P_s + t lands heavier on the side that cannot walk away. A rent ceiling, meanwhile, freezes the price but creates a queue. Push the sliders and see for yourself.

scenes.title: Two Firms Watching Each Other
scenes.summary: A town with only two cola firms. The price is set by their combined output: P = a - b(q_1 + q_2). Once the rival picks q_2, your best move comes from the reply rule q_1 = \frac{a - c - b q_2}{2b}. The market settles where the two replies cross.

scenes.title: The Factory and the River
scenes.summary: A factory dumps waste in a river, and the fishing village downstream pays for it. The factory's cost MPC plus the river's damage MD is society's true cost, MSC = MPC + MD. The market hears only MPC and makes too much — the right tax closes the gap.

scenes.title: Tragedy of the Shared Pasture
scenes.summary: The pasture belongs to everyone; the sheep belong to each herder. A sheep's worth v(S) = a - bS falls as the total flock S grows, yet each herder counts only their own animals. The more herders share the field, the further the total overshoots the optimum — and the pasture's profit evaporates.

scenes.title: Why Does the Superstar Earn So Much?
scenes.summary: A star singer's fee and land by a new station split the same way. Of the payment w for a factor, what it could earn elsewhere is transfer earnings; the pure bonus on top is economic rent. The steeper the supply w = c + sq — the harder the factor is to replace — the more of the payment hardens into rent.

scenes.title: The Amusement Park Pricing Puzzle
scenes.summary: There are three ways to sell the same ride. Per-ride pricing charges like a monopolist, a flat pass makes extra rides free and invites overuse, and a two-part tariff splits the bill into two pieces, F + pq. Price rides at cost and collect the surplus at the gate, and the waste vanishes — but so does the guest's share.

scenes.title: Three Ways to Tax
scenes.summary: One market, three taxes. A lump-sum bill L never enters the price decision and leaves trade untouched, a specific tax t drives a fixed wedge per unit, and an ad valorem tax \tau stretches the buyer's price to (1 + \tau) times the seller's. Only wedged taxes shrink trade and leave a triangle behind.

scenes.title: Why Higher Prices Mean Buying Less — Except When They Don't
scenes.summary: When a price rises, the response splits in two: a substitution effect SE away from the pricier good, and an income effect IE from being effectively poorer. Usually they point the same way — but for an inferior good like instant noodles the income effect pushes back, and for a survival staple like rice it can win outright: the Giffen case, where a higher price means buying more.

scenes.title: Why Good Used Cars Never Show Up
scenes.summary: Why are good used cars never on the market? Only the seller knows the quality \theta. At price p the cars offered average just p/2 in quality, so buyers offer at most k times that. If k < 2, each round shrinks the price by a factor of \frac{k}{2} and it spirals to 0 — the market vanishes even though every trade would have made both sides better off. The same structure wears three costumes. Information asymmetry: Akerlof's lemons market itself — only the seller knows the quality. Adverse selection: in health insurance, higher premiums drive out the healthy first, which pushes premiums higher still — Washington State's individual health-insurance market actually collapsed this way in the 1990s. Moral hazard: behavior changes after the deal — in the 1980s, U.S. savings and loans, trusting deposit insurance, piled into risky loans and failed in droves.

scenes.title: Winning the Auction, Losing Money
scenes.summary: Why the winner of a coin-jar auction is the biggest loser. Each bidder's signal scatters within \pm d of the true value V, and the winner is whoever saw the rosiest signal. With N bidders the top signal averages V + d \cdot \frac{N-1}{N+1} — winning itself is the news that you overestimated the most.

scenes.title: Preference Relations and Axioms
scenes.summary: See preferences on the 2-good plane. Switching the utility family redraws the indifference map, and two bundles A, B are ranked instantly. Watch what breaks when completeness or transitivity fails.

scenes.title: Choice Rules and WARP
scenes.summary: Pick bundles yourself in two budget situations. If each situation could have afforded the other’s choice — that violates the Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP).

scenes.title: The Budget Set
scenes.summary: The affordable region fixed by prices p and wealth w: B_{p,w} = \{x \ge 0 : p\cdot x \le w\}. Move the sliders and the budget line rotates and shifts.

scenes.title: Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve
scenes.summary: The Cobb-Douglas demand curve x_1(p_1) = aw/p_1. The price slider slides along it, and the \lambda slider proves homogeneity x(\lambda p, \lambda w) = x(p, w) numerically.

scenes.title: Indifference Curves and MRS
scenes.summary: The indifference map of Cobb-Douglas utility. Move the reference bundle and the whole map redraws; the marginal rate of substitution MRS = \frac{a}{1-a}\frac{x_2}{x_1} at that point reads off as the tangent slope.

scenes.title: Utility Maximization
scenes.summary: The optimum is where the budget line touches an indifference curve. Move prices and wealth and the optimum slides; the first-order condition MRS = p_1/p_2 holds at every moment, verified numerically.

scenes.title: The Slutsky Decomposition
scenes.summary: Why does demand fall when the price rises — split into substitution and income effects. Switch between Slutsky compensation (afford the old bundle) and Hicks compensation (keep the old utility) and see how the two decompositions differ.

scenes.title: Expenditure Minimization and Duality
scenes.summary: Achieving target utility as cheaply as possible — the tangency of isocost lines and the indifference curve. Turn on the "UMP mirror" and the utility-maximizing bundle at w = e(p, u) lands exactly on Hicksian demand. That coincidence is duality.

scenes.title: Aggregating Demand
scenes.summary: Add three consumers’ Cobb-Douglas demand curves into one aggregate curve. Walras’ law and homogeneity of degree zero survive — move each demand and check.

scenes.title: The Representative Consumer
scenes.summary: Shift wealth between two identical-taste consumers however you like — the aggregate demand curve never moves. When demand depends only on total wealth, a representative consumer exists.

scenes.title: Isoquants
scenes.summary: The isoquant map of q = z_1^{\alpha} z_2^{\beta}. Move the reference input point and the MRTS MRTS = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}\frac{z_2}{z_1} reads off as the tangent slope.

scenes.title: Cost Minimization
scenes.summary: The cheapest input mix for target output q — the tangency of the isoquant and an isocost line. Move factor prices and watch conditional factor demands slide.

scenes.title: Cost Curves
scenes.summary: Marginal, average, and average-variable cost from a cubic total cost. The marginal cost curve passes exactly through the minimum of the average cost curve.

scenes.title: Expected Utility
scenes.summary: A lottery L is worth the expectation of Bernoulli utility, U(L) = \sum p_n u(x_n). See the Jensen gap between the expected value and expected utility on a concave utility curve.

scenes.title: Measuring Risk Aversion
scenes.summary: Raise the risk-aversion coefficient \gamma in CRRA utility and the certainty equivalent drifts away from the expected value — the risk premium grows. The Arrow-Pratt measure reads off alongside.

scenes.title: Demand for Insurance
scenes.summary: The contingent-claims diagram: wealth in the loss state vs the no-loss state. At a fair premium the optimum is full insurance on the 45-degree line — loading on the premium slides it to partial insurance.

scenes.title: Normal-Form Games and Best Responses
scenes.summary: Look directly at the 2 \times 2 payoff matrix. Mark player 1's best response in each column and player 2's in each row; the cells where both are bold — the starred cells — are exactly the pure-strategy Nash equilibria.

scenes.title: Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Condition
scenes.summary: When player 2 mixes with probability q, player 1's expected payoff from each pure strategy is a line in q. At their crossing q^* player 1 is indifferent — the only q that can appear in a mixed equilibrium.

scenes.title: Zero-Sum Games and Minimax
scenes.summary: One player's gain is the other's loss. Edit the payoff matrix and compare maximin with minimax: equality means a saddle point (pure equilibrium); a gap means a fully mixed equilibrium and a value of the game.

scenes.title: Nash Equilibrium and Best-Response Correspondences
scenes.summary: Draw both correspondences in the (q, p) plane: blue is player 1's optimal mix on q, orange is player 2's on p. Their intersections are the Nash equilibria — pure ones at the corners, the mixed one starred inside.

scenes.title: Iterated Elimination of Strictly Dominated Strategies
scenes.summary: Delete what a rational player would never play, round by round. Push the round slider and C \to M \to D vanish in turn, until only U remains and player 2 answers with L.

scenes.title: Extensive-Form Games and Backward Induction
scenes.summary: Draw the entry game as a tree. Push the slider to solve it backwards: the incumbent accommodates (1 beats -1), the entrant enters. The pruned Fight branch is a specimen of a non-credible threat.

scenes.title: Repeated Games and Cooperation
scenes.summary: Play grim-trigger in the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma. Moving the discount factor \delta flips which curve is on top — "always cooperate" vs "deviate once" — and cooperation survives in the shaded region right of \delta^* = \frac{T-R}{T-P}.

scenes.title: Supply, Demand, and Equilibrium
scenes.summary: The competitive equilibrium is where demand P = A - Q meets supply P = C + Q. Raise the per-unit tax t and a wedge opens between the buyer and seller prices, splitting consumer surplus, producer surplus, revenue, and deadweight loss in real time.

scenes.title: Tax vs Quota: Deadweight Loss
scenes.summary: Taxes and quotas both shrink trade, but the lost welfare has the same shape. Switch instruments and watch the deadweight-loss triangle keep its area, while the transfer becomes tax revenue or quota rent.

scenes.title: Externalities and the Pigouvian Tax
scenes.summary: Private marginal cost MPC sits below social marginal cost MSC — that gap is the externality. The market overproduces up to Q_p, and welfare equal to the red triangle vanishes. Flip the Pigouvian tax \tau = MD(Q_s) switch and the dashed cost curve aims exactly at the social optimum.

scenes.title: Public Goods and Free-Riding
scenes.summary: Public-good demands sum vertically, not horizontally — everyone consumes the same unit at once. The Samuelson optimum is where the vertical sum meets marginal cost, but in the voluntary-contribution Nash equilibrium the weaker-demand side free-rides and supply falls short.

scenes.title: Monopoly: Marginal Revenue and Deadweight Loss
scenes.summary: The monopolist sets price by sliding down the demand curve — which is why marginal revenue MR falls twice as fast as demand. Profit peaks where MR = MC, but the red triangle of welfare on the unproduced output evaporates.

scenes.title: Cournot Oligopoly
scenes.summary: Each firm picks its best output against its rivals' — the reaction functions cross at the Cournot-Nash equilibrium. Push the firm-count N slider: at N = 1 it is monopoly, and as N grows it converges to competition.

scenes.title: Price Discrimination
scenes.summary: The art of charging different prices in different markets. Third-degree sets MR_i = MC per market; first-degree converts all consumer surplus into profit. But third-degree deadweight loss can exceed the uniform-price one — check the calculation that breaks the folk wisdom.

scenes.title: The Edgeworth Box and Competitive Equilibrium
scenes.summary: Endowment, offer curves, and the contract curve inside the two-consumer box. At the equilibrium price p_1 the budget line touches both indifference curves at once — that tangency is the competitive equilibrium. The thick segment is the core.

scenes.title: The Two Welfare Theorems
scenes.summary: Walk along the utility possibility frontier. Competitive equilibrium (CE) sits on the frontier — the First Theorem. Pick another Pareto optimum with the slider and the supporting price plus the lump-sum transfer T that decentralizes it are computed — the Second Theorem.

scenes.title: Tatonnement Dynamics
scenes.summary: The auctioneer raises and lowers the price watching excess demand: p_{t+1} = p_t + k\, z(p_t). Raising the speed k quickens convergence — until past a threshold it diverges instead. An overeager auctioneer destabilizes the market.

scenes.title: Excess Demand: Existence and Uniqueness
scenes.summary: Where the excess demand curve z_1(p_1) crosses zero is equilibrium. In the Cobb-Douglas economy there is always exactly one (gross substitutes), and Walras' law p \cdot z = 0 holds. Switch to illustrative mode and there can be three equilibria — uniqueness is not free.

scenes.title: Shrinking of the Core (Debreu–Scarf)
scenes.summary: Replicating the economy creates new coalitions that slice the core down. Watch the core interval shrink to the single competitive point across N = 1, 2, 4, 8 replicas — in a large economy, core and competitive equilibrium coincide.

scenes.title: Blocking Coalitions
scenes.summary: Move the allocation with the sliders. Violate individual rationality and \{1\} or \{2\} blocks alone; be Pareto inefficient and the grand coalition blocks via the lens region. The allocations that survive are exactly the core.

scenes.title: Arrow–Debreu Equilibrium
scenes.summary: An Edgeworth box in state-contingent consumption space. With no aggregate risk, both consumers sit on the 45-degree line in equilibrium — full insurance (mutuality principle). Move the aggregate-risk slider and everyone tracks the aggregate.

scenes.title: State Prices and Scarcity
scenes.summary: Probabilities vs. state prices across three states, side by side. State prices are marginal-utility-weighted probabilities, not raw probabilities — a dollar in the scarcest state costs the most (numbers above the bars: q_s/\pi_s).

scenes.title: Intertemporal Equilibrium and the Interest Rate
scenes.summary: Trade period 1 for period 2 along the present-value budget line. At the market-clearing rate 1 + r = E_2/(\delta E_1), the period-1-rich consumer becomes the lender.

scenes.title: Overlapping Generations and the Golden Rule
scenes.summary: Money links trades between generations that never meet. The monetary steady state and the golden rule (e/2, e/2) coincide only at \delta = 1 — with infinite horizons, the First Welfare Theorem's conclusion can fail.

scenes.title: Arrow's Theorem
scenes.summary: Switch preference profiles and aggregation rules. On the Condorcet profile majority rule cycles; under Borda, removing an irrelevant alternative flips the ranking (IIA violation). No rule satisfies all four conditions.

scenes.title: Social Welfare Functions
scenes.summary: Maximize CES social welfare over the utility possibility set. Sliding \rho from 1 to -\infty moves the optimum from the utilitarian point (9.22, 6.40) to the Rawls point (7.68, 7.68).

scenes.title: The Value of Information
scenes.summary: An investment decision under state \theta \in \{\text{good}, \text{bad}\}. Move the signal accuracy q of s \in \{h, l\} and the posteriors and optimal actions after each signal change; the value of information \text{VoI} = \text{EV}_{\text{with}} - \text{EV}_{\text{no}} reads off as bars. The investment rule P(\text{good} \mid s) > L/(R+L) is verified numerically at every moment.

scenes.title: Optimal Sequential Search
scenes.summary: Each round draws an offer X \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 100] at cost c. The indifference condition c = (M - r)^2/(2M) pins down the reservation value r^*, and the stopping rule "keep searching while the best offer is below r^*" is optimal. The V(r) curve peaks exactly at (r^*, r^*).

scenes.title: Akerlof's Lemons Market
scenes.summary: Only the seller knows the quality. At price p only cars with q \le p are offered, so average quality is p/2 and the buyer's willingness to pay is WTP(p) = mp/2. When m < 2, WTP(p) < p always holds, the price unravels to 0, and the gains from trade vanish entirely.

scenes.title: Education Signaling
scenes.summary: When productivity cannot be shown directly, high-productivity workers signal with education. Because education costs e/\theta differ by type (single crossing), the low type cannot follow: separating equilibria exist for e^* \in [1, 2], and at the least-cost equilibrium e^* = 1 the signaling cost 0.5 is pure waste.

scenes.title: Screening Menus
scenes.summary: The uninformed side (a monopolist) moves first with a menu, and types self-select. No distortion at the top: q_H = 2. The bottom is cut to q_L = \theta_L - \frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}(\theta_H-\theta_L), and the high type pockets an information rent of (\theta_H-\theta_L)q_L.

scenes.title: Moral Hazard and Incentives
scenes.summary: When effort is unobservable, a flat wage invites shirking. The optimal contract (w_L, w_H) is where incentive compatibility (p_1 - p_0)(u_H - u_L) = c meets the participation constraint. Raise risk tolerance \alpha and the pay-for-performance slope flattens — the risk-sharing versus incentives tradeoff, made visible.

scenes.title: Which Effort to Implement
scenes.summary: Incentivizing high effort has a price. Profit \Pi_1(c) falls as the effort cost c rises, while low-effort profit \Pi_0 stays flat. Buying incentives pays only left of the crossing c^* — incentives are worth it only while the effort cost, hence the risk premium, is small enough.

scenes.title: The Revelation Principle and Optimal Auctions
scenes.summary: One seller, one buyer with value v \sim U[0,1]. The revelation principle lets us study only direct mechanisms: sell iff the report meets the reserve r, and the winner pays r. The positive region of the virtual value \psi(v) = 2v - 1 is exactly expected revenue R(r) = r - r^2, maximized at r^* = 0.5 with 0.25. Run the lie checker and truth always wins.

scenes.title: Second-Price Auction: Truth-Telling Is Dominant
scenes.summary: A second-price auction against one opponent (v_o \sim U[0,100], truthful). The expected payoff of bidding b is U(b; v) = (vb - b^2/2)/100, a parabola peaking at b = v. Overbidding creates wins that cost more than the value; underbidding forfeits wins you could have had — the loss is exactly (v-b)^2/200.

scenes.title: Maskin Monotonicity
scenes.summary: Two agents, three alternatives X = \{a, b, c\}. If a rule f picks x at \theta and x falls for no one at \theta', then f(\theta') must still be x — a necessary condition for Nash implementation. The dictatorial rule passes; the bottom-choice rule earns a red violation.

terms.definition: How many percent quantity changes when price changes by 1\% — a gauge of responsiveness. Steeper curves are more elastic.
The boundary of affordable bundles with income m — p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 = m. The happiest point on this line is the choice.
A binary relation \succsim on a set X of alternatives. x \succsim y means the consumer likes x at least as much as y. A rational preference is complete and transitive.
The axiom that for any two alternatives x, y, either x \succsim y or y \succsim x (or both) holds — the consumer can compare any pair.
The axiom that x \succsim y and y \succsim z imply x \succsim z — it guarantees the consistency of preferences.
x \sim y when x \succsim y and y \succsim x both hold — the two alternatives are equally good.
A function u: X \to \mathbb{R} representing \succsim: x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y). Any monotone transform represents the same preference, so it is an ordinal concept.
A rule assigning to each budget set (a subset of feasible alternatives) B the set C(B) \subseteq B of alternatives actually chosen.
The consistency condition: if x is chosen when y was available, then x must not be available whenever y is chosen. Choice derived from rational preferences satisfies WARP.
The set of affordable consumption bundles at prices p and wealth w: B_{p,w} = \{x \ge 0 : p \cdot x \le w\}. Its boundary is the budget line.
Under locally nonsatiated preferences the optimum spends the whole budget: p \cdot x = w. If money were left over, a better bundle would be affordable.
The good serving as the price standard — its price is normalized to 1. Demand is unaffected by the numeraire choice thanks to homogeneity in prices and wealth.
The solution x(p, w) of the utility maximization problem — demand as a function of prices and wealth. Also called Marshallian demand.
terms.sceneTitle: Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve

terms.definition: Walrasian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in prices and wealth: x(\alpha p, \alpha w) = x(p, w). A proportional rise in all prices and income changes nothing real.
terms.sceneTitle: Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve

terms.definition: The set \{x : u(x) = \bar{u}\} of bundles yielding equal utility. Under monotonicity and convexity it slopes downward and is convex to the origin.

The slope (in absolute value) of an indifference curve — how much of good 1 the consumer needs at the margin to give up one unit of good 2. MRS = \frac{\partial u / \partial x_1}{\partial u / \partial x_2}.
\max_x u(x) subject to p \cdot x \le w. Its solution is Walrasian (Marshallian) demand x(p, w); its value is indirect utility v(p, w).
The value function of the UMP, v(p, w) = \max_{p \cdot x \le w} u(x). Nonincreasing in prices, nondecreasing in wealth, homogeneous of degree zero.
The formula recovering Walrasian demand from indirect utility: x_l(p, w) = -\frac{\partial v / \partial p_l}{\partial v / \partial w}.

Decomposes a price effect into substitution and income effects: \frac{\partial x_l}{\partial p_k} = \frac{\partial h_l}{\partial p_k} - \frac{\partial x_l}{\partial w} x_k. The substitution effect is always nonpositive.
The effect of a price change on demand holding utility compensated — the slope of Hicksian demand. Always nonpositive for the own price.
The effect of a price change on demand through changed real purchasing power. Same direction as the substitution effect for normal goods, opposite for inferior goods.
The solution h(p, u) of the expenditure minimization problem — the cheapest bundle achieving utility u. Homogeneous of degree zero in prices, nonincreasing in own price.
A good whose demand rises when its price rises — happens when a strong inferior-good income effect overwhelms the substitution effect.
\min_x p \cdot x subject to u(x) \ge u. Its solution is Hicksian demand h(p, u); its value is the expenditure function e(p, u).
The value function of the EMP, e(p, u). Homogeneous of degree one in prices, concave, nondecreasing — and yields Hicksian demand via Shephard's lemma.
Differentiating the expenditure function in a price gives Hicksian demand: h_l(p, u) = \frac{\partial e(p, u)}{\partial p_l}.
The UMP and EMP mirror each other: h(p, u) = x(p, e(p, u)), x(p, w) = h(p, v(p, w)). Each problem's solution recovers the other's.
The sum of individual demands X(p) = \sum_i x^i(p, w_i). Walras' law and homogeneity of degree zero survive aggregation, but WARP generally does not.
A fictional consumer whose demand reproduces aggregate demand. Exists (independently of the wealth distribution) when indirect utilities take the Gorman form.
v_i(p, w_i) = a_i(p) + b(p) w_i — indirect utility with a common marginal utility of wealth b(p). Makes aggregate demand depend only on total wealth.
The set \{(z_1, z_2) : f(z_1, z_2) = q\} of input bundles producing output q. Convex to the origin when the production function is concave.
The slope (in absolute value) of an isoquant — how much of input 1 marginally replaces one unit of input 2 holding output fixed. MRTS = \frac{\partial f / \partial z_1}{\partial f / \partial z_2}.
How output scales when all inputs scale by t: increasing if f(tz) > t f(z), constant if equal, decreasing if smaller.
The solution z(w, q) of the cost minimization problem — the inputs chosen at factor prices w to produce target output q.
c(w, q) = \min_{f(z) \ge q} w \cdot z — the minimum cost of producing q. Homogeneous of degree one in factor prices, concave, nondecreasing.
The extra cost of making one more unit — discretely MC = \Delta C / \Delta q, continuously MC(q) = c'(q). Profit maximization sets price equal to marginal cost, pinning down supply.
AC(q) = c(q)/q — cost per unit. The marginal cost curve passes through the minimum of the average cost curve.
A probability distribution over outcomes C — the mathematical form of an uncertain prospect. A simple lottery puts probabilities on finitely many outcomes.
The utility of a lottery U(L) = \sum_n p_n u(x_n) — the expectation of Bernoulli utility u. Under continuity and independence, preferences take this form.
If L \succsim L' then \alpha L + (1-\alpha)L'' \succsim \alpha L' + (1-\alpha)L'' for any L'' and \alpha \in (0,1) — a common mixture never reverses the ranking. The Allais paradox breaks it.
Preferring a sure amount over a lottery with the same expected value — equivalent to a concave Bernoulli utility u.
The sure amount c indifferent to lottery L: u(c) = \mathbb{E}[u(L)]. For a risk averter, c < \mathbb{E}[L].
\pi = \mathbb{E}[L] - c — the slice of expected value the agent would give up to avoid the lottery. The price of risk aversion.
The coefficient of absolute risk aversion r_A(x) = -u''(x)/u'(x) — a local gauge of how strongly risk is disliked.
A premium equal to the expected loss — zero expected profit for the insurer. At a fair premium, a risk averter buys full insurance.
A strategy profile where no player can gain by unilaterally deviating, holding others' strategies fixed. Each strategy is a best response to the rest.
A strategy that randomizes over pure strategies. In equilibrium every pure strategy in the mix yields the same expected payoff (the indifference condition).
terms.sceneTitle: Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Condition

terms.definition: A strategy that is best no matter what others do. Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IEDS) simplifies a game but can miss Nash equilibria.
terms.sceneTitle: Iterated Elimination of Strictly Dominated Strategies

terms.definition: A strategy profile that is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame. It rules out non-credible threats and is found by backward induction.
The gap between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay — the triangle under demand and above price.
Total surplus destroyed when quantity deviates from the efficient level (taxes, monopoly) — measured by the Harberger triangle.
A tax that corrects an externality — setting \tau = MD(Q_s) equal to marginal damage brings the market back to the social optimum.
Non-rival, non-excludable goods. The Samuelson condition (vertical sum of marginal benefits = marginal cost) sets optimal supply, but free-riding causes underprovision.
A single seller maximizing profit at MR = MC — price exceeds marginal cost and deadweight loss arises.
terms.sceneTitle: Monopoly: Marginal Revenue and Deadweight Loss

terms.definition: An oligopoly model where firms choose quantities simultaneously. Reaction functions intersect at the Cournot-Nash equilibrium, converging to competition as the number of firms grows.
A box plotting two consumers' endowments and indifference curves together. Points on the contract curve are Pareto efficient allocations.
terms.sceneTitle: The Edgeworth Box and Competitive Equilibrium

terms.definition: A state where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. The First Welfare Theorem says competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
The set of allocations no coalition can profitably block. In a replica economy the core shrinks to competitive equilibrium as the economy grows (Debreu-Scarf).
Equilibrium with complete markets in state-contingent commodities. With no aggregate risk, full insurance (risk sharing) obtains.
No social welfare function satisfies universality, Pareto, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and non-dictatorship all at once.
Market unraveling when the informed side selects in — Akerlof's market for lemons is the canonical case.
Costly revelation of type by the informed side — Spence's education model yields a separating equilibrium.
The problem that the agent's post-contract action (effort) is unobservable. Risk sharing trades off against incentives under the incentive-compatibility constraint.
The condition that truth-telling is optimal for participants. By the revelation principle, design can be restricted to direct mechanisms.
terms.sceneTitle: The Revelation Principle and Optimal Auctions

terms.definition: The second-price auction — bidding truthfully is a weakly dominant strategy. The canonical incentive-compatible mechanism.

exercises.statement: Gasoline demand is Q_d = 12 - P and supply is Q_s = 2P. Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
The lunch budget grows to m = 60. Food 1 costs p_1 = 6, food 2 costs p_2 = 8. What is the best bundle satisfying the budget equation p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = m?
The cafe has fixed cost 20 and marginal cost MC = 4 + 2q. If the coffee price drops from P = 20 to 16, what happens to the best quantity and profit?

Two cola firms face the price P = 18 - (q_1 + q_2) and a cost of 3 per bottle. In the Cournot equilibrium, how much does each firm make and what is the price? Compare the total with monopoly and competition.
A star athlete's market has demand w = 18 - q and supply w = 6 + 2q. Find the payment w and quantity q, then split the total payment into economic rent and transfer earnings.

A gym member's visit demand is q = 16 - P and each visit costs the gym 2. If the gym prices visits at cost, 2, and lives off the membership fee alone, how many visits does the member make, and what is the most the gym can charge per month?
A consumer with a lunch budget of 40 and food 2 at 8 meets a half-price sale on food 1 (4 down to 2). How much does food 1 grow, and how does the increase split into substitution and income effects?
A tax t = 4 hits a market with demand Q_d = 10 - 0.5P and supply Q_s = P. How is the tax split between buyers and sellers, and how large is the deadweight loss?
A sheep is worth v(S) = 10 - S and costs 2. If the herders grow to 9, what happens to the total flock and the pasture's total profit? What per-herder limit would restore the optimum?

Shops in a market with demand P = 12 - Q and supply P = 2 + Q are charged a yearly license fee of 10 — a lump-sum tax. What are the quantity, revenue, and deadweight loss? Compare with a specific tax of t = 3, and explain what happens if the fee rises to 15.

In a used-car market, quality spreads evenly from 0 to 100 and buyers value a car at 1.6 times its quality (k = 1.6). Find the first price, the shrink factor per round, the number of cuts before the price falls below 10, and the gains from trade that vanish. How large must k be for the market to survive?
A consumer reports (5, 1) \succ (3, 3) and (3, 3) \succ (2, 4). If the preference relation \succsim is complete and transitive, what can be said about (5, 1) versus (2, 4)?

Consider a perfect-substitutes consumer with u(x_1, x_2) = x_1 + x_2. Find the marginal rate of substitution MRS = \frac{\partial u / \partial x_1}{\partial u / \partial x_2} and write the equation of the indifference curve through (6, 6). Is B = (9, 4) preferred to A = (6, 6)?
The consumer chose x = (20, 40) at (p, w) = ((1, 1), 60) and y = (25, 25) at (p', w') = ((3, 1), 100). Compute the revealed-preference relations and decide whether WARP is violated.

Pairwise choices over the three bundles A = (4, 4), B = (5, 2), C = (2, 5) came out as follows (each pair has a unique winner): A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. Prove that no complete and transitive preference relation \succsim rationalizes all three choices.
With p_1 = 2, p_2 = 1, w = 60, find the two intercepts and the slope of the budget line.
At p = (1, 1), w = 60 the bundle (30, 30) lies on the budget line. When p_1 rises to 2, is this bundle still affordable? Describe the geometric change of the budget line as well.
With u(x_1, x_2) = x_1^{1/4} x_2^{3/4}, p_1 = 2, p_2 = 1, w = 80, find x_1(p, w) and verify that doubling all prices and wealth leaves demand unchanged.
For \lambda > 0, prove that B(\lambda p, \lambda w) = B(p, w), and deduce directly from the definition of the UMP that Walrasian demand x(p, w) is homogeneous of degree zero.
With u(x_1, x_2) = x_1^{1/3} x_2^{2/3}, p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, w = 120, find Walrasian demand x(p, w) and indirect utility v(p, w).
Starting from the budget line with p_1 = 1, p_2 = 2, w = 100, how does the budget line move when w rises to 150? Find the new optimum of a Cobb-Douglas consumer with a = 1/2.
Let u = x_1^{1/4} x_2^{3/4}, p_2 = 1, w = 80. When p_1 rises from 1 to 4, compute the substitution, income, and total effects of the Slutsky decomposition.
Prove directly from the definition of the EMP that the expenditure function e(p, u) is homogeneous of degree one in prices.
Prove with the Slutsky equation that a Giffen good cannot arise under Cobb-Douglas utility.
Prove the duality identity e(p, v(p, w)) = w from the definitions of the UMP and EMP (assume interior solutions and local nonsatiation).
Three Cobb-Douglas consumers have parameters a = (0.4, 0.5, 0.6), wealths w_i = 50, and p_2 = 1. At p_1 = 2, find each consumer's x_1^i and aggregate demand X_1.

Suppose each consumer i satisfies Walras' law p \cdot x^i(p, w_i) = w_i (no assumption on the functional form of demand). Prove that aggregate demand X(p) = \sum_i x^i(p, w_i) satisfies p \cdot X(p) = \sum_i w_i.

Two identical-taste Cobb-Douglas consumers with a = 1/2, total wealth W = 100, p_1 = 1, p_2 = 1. Compute X_1 for the splits s = 0.25 and s = 0.75, and verify that individual demands change while aggregate demand does not.

Suppose I consumers have indirect utilities of the Gorman form v_i(p, w_i) = \alpha_i(p) + b(p)\,w_i with a common b(p) > 0. Use Roy's identity to derive each demand, prove that aggregate demand X(p) depends only on total wealth W = \sum_i w_i, and exhibit a representative consumer's indirect utility reproducing it.
For the production function q = z_1^{1/3} z_2^{2/3}, compute the MRTS at (z_1, z_2) = (2, 8).
With w_1 = 3, w_2 = 1, q = 10, \alpha = \beta = 1/2, find the conditional factor demands z(w, q) and the minimum cost c(w, q).
For C(q) = 40 + 30q - 4q^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}q^3, find the output minimizing average variable cost and the marginal cost there.

Let \alpha = 0.3, \beta = 0.4 (decreasing returns), w_1 = w_2 = 1. Compute c(w, 16)/c(w, 8) from the conditional-demand formula, explain why it exceeds 2, and state the degree of homogeneity of c(w, q) in q in general.
A consumer with u(x) = \sqrt{x} evaluates a lottery paying 144 with probability 1/2 and 36 with probability 1/2. Find the certainty equivalent and the risk premium.
Show that in CRRA utility u(x) = x^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma), the (normalized) utility converges to log utility as \gamma \to 1: \lim_{\gamma \to 1} \frac{x^{1-\gamma} - 1}{1-\gamma} = \ln x.

A consumer with W = 100, loss L = 60 (probability \pi = 0.3), and u(x) = \sqrt{x} buys \beta coverage at premium rate p per dollar. Differentiate expected utility with respect to \beta to derive the first-order condition and solve for \beta^*(p). Check the value at p = 0.3.

Two CRRA consumers A (\gamma_A = 0.5) and B (\gamma_B = 2) evaluate the 50-50 lottery (150, 50). Compute each certainty equivalent and risk premium, and explain via the Arrow-Pratt measure who is more risk averse.
In the Prisoner's Dilemma \begin{matrix} & C & D \\ C & (3,3) & (0,5) \\ D & (5,0) & (1,1) \end{matrix}, find each player's strictly dominant strategy and the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

Find the fully mixed Nash equilibrium (p^*, q^*) of the Battle of the Sexes \begin{matrix} & O & F \\ O & (3,2) & (0,0) \\ F & (0,0) & (2,3) \end{matrix} and compute each player's equilibrium expected payoff.
For the zero-sum game \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix} (player 1's payoffs), find maximin and minimax, confirm no saddle point, then compute the mixed equilibrium and the value.
Prove that a 2 \times 2 zero-sum game with no pure-strategy saddle point has a unique fully mixed Nash equilibrium, and derive its value v = \frac{ad-bc}{a-b-c+d}.
Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria of the Stag Hunt \begin{matrix} & S & H \\ S & (4,4) & (0,3) \\ H & (3,0) & (3,3) \end{matrix} and rank them by Pareto dominance.

In \begin{matrix} & L & C & R \\ U & (4,3) & (5,1) & (6,2) \\ M & (2,1) & (8,4) & (3,6) \\ D & (3,0) & (9,6) & (2,8) \end{matrix}, iteratively eliminate strictly dominated strategies and find the final outcome.
Show Matching Pennies \begin{matrix} & H & T \\ H & (1,-1) & (-1,1) \\ T & (-1,1) & (1,-1) \end{matrix} has no pure-strategy equilibrium, and find its unique (mixed) equilibrium.
Prove that the set of strategy profiles surviving iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies contains every Nash equilibrium.
Find the subgame-perfect equilibrium of the entry game (Stay Out → (0,2); after Enter, Accommodate → (1,1), Fight → (-1,-1)) by backward induction.
Show that (Stay Out, Fight-if-enter) is a Nash equilibrium but not subgame perfect, and explain the difference between the concepts.

In the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with T = 4, R = 3, P = 1, find the minimum discount factor \delta^* for grim-trigger to sustain cooperation, and decide whether cooperation holds at \delta = 0.5.

Prove by backward induction that finitely repeating ( T times) a stage game with a unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium has a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium: repeat the stage equilibrium every period.
In a market with demand P = 12 - Q and supply P = 4 + Q, find the competitive equilibrium (Q^*, P^*) and the consumer and producer surplus at it.
With demand P = 12 - Q and supply P = 4 + Q, a per-unit tax t = 3 is imposed. Find the deadweight loss and the tax revenue.
In the same market, find the deadweight loss of a quota \bar{Q} = 2, and the tax rate that gives the same deadweight loss.
In the linear supply-demand model, prove geometrically from the triangle that DWL = t^2/(2(B+D)), and explain why doubling the tax rate quadruples the deadweight loss.
With demand P = 10 - Q, MPC = 2 + Q, and MD = 1 + Q, write down the social marginal cost curve and find the social optimum Q_s.
With demand P = 10 - Q, MPC = 2 + Q, and MD = 1 + Q, find the Pigouvian tax rate and verify that the market quantity under that tax equals the social optimum.
For a public good with D_1: P = 12 - G, D_2: P = 6 - G, c = 4, find the voluntary-contribution Nash equilibrium (g_1, g_2) and the Samuelson optimum G^*, and compare them.

Suppose the two consumers have equal demand slopes (b_1 = b_2 = b). Express in terms of a_1, a_2, c the condition under which the voluntary-contribution Nash equilibrium falls short of the Samuelson optimum, and prove it.
With demand P = 14 - Q and c = 2, find the monopolist's profit-maximizing (Q_m, P_m) and its profit.
In a 3-firm Cournot market with demand P = 10 - Q and c = 2, find the symmetric Nash equilibrium per-firm output, total output, and price.
With n = 100 identical consumers each having demand P = 12 - q and c = 2, find the profit-maximizing two-part tariff (fixed fee F + per-unit price p).
In the Cournot equilibrium with linear demand P = A - BQ and N symmetric firms, prove that each firm's Lerner index \frac{P - c}{P} equals its market share divided by demand elasticity.
In an economy with a_1 = 1/3, a_2 = 2/3, W = (12, 12), e^1 = (9, 3), find the equilibrium price p_1 (with p_2 = 1).
Show that the endowment itself can be Pareto inefficient: with a_1 = a_2 = 1/2, W = (10, 10), e^1 = (9, 1), exhibit an allocation that strictly improves both consumers.
In the symmetric economy (a_1 = a_2 = 1/2, W = (10,10), e^1 = (7,3)), in which direction must the lump-sum transfer flow to decentralize the Pareto optimum x^1 = (4, 4)? Find its size.

Prove that the core always contains the competitive equilibrium. (Hint: suppose the equilibrium allocation x^* were outside the core — which coalition could block it? Consider that coalition's budget at equilibrium prices.)
In a market with D(p) = 36/p and S(p) = 2 + 2p, find the equilibrium price and determine whether tatonnement raises or lowers the price at p = 2.
Explain the intuition for why the gross substitutes condition \partial z_l / \partial p_k > 0 (l \ne k) implies uniqueness of equilibrium in a 2-good economy.
In an L-good economy, prove with Walras' law that if excess demand is zero in L-1 markets, it is zero in the remaining market too.
In a Cobb-Douglas exchange economy, show that z_1(p_1) \to +\infty as p_1 \to 0^+, and explain why this is the heart of the existence argument.
Explain via strict concavity why a core allocation in a replica economy satisfies "equal treatment" — i.e., same-type consumers get the same bundle.
In the symmetric economy with N = 2, show that coalition (2, 1)'s per-capita endowment is (17/3, 13/3), and explain the intuition for why it blocks x^1_1 = 5.42.
Explain (with this chapter's numerical example) that the core always contains the competitive allocation, but not conversely.
Discuss how the Debreu–Scarf theorem connects to the claim that "as the economy grows large, the price mechanism is justified."
With log utility, \pi_1 = 0.4, E_1 = 8, E_2 = 12, find the state price ratio q_1/q_2.
When both consumers' endowments are already fully insured (e^1 = (5, 5)) with no aggregate risk, show that no trade occurs in Arrow–Debreu equilibrium.
Discuss whether risk aversion \gamma affects state prices. (Hint: compare the log-utility formula with the \gamma \ne 1 case.)
In an economy with S states, L goods, and T dates, find how many contingent commodities an Arrow–Debreu equilibrium needs for complete markets, and give the number for S = 2, L = 2, T = 2.
With e^1 = (8, 2) and r = 0.5, find consumer 1's present-value budget set and give both intercepts of the budget line.
From 1 + r = E_2/(\delta E_1), explain what happens to the equilibrium interest rate when all consumers become more impatient (\delta falls).
In an OLG economy with \delta = 0.75, e = 12, find the steady-state savings rate s/e.
Explain what it means for money to be "essential" in the OLG economy, via the steady-state allocation.
For the mixed profile (1: A > B > C, 2: A > C > B, 3: B > A > C), find the Borda scores and the plurality outcome.
Explain why all four rules (Condorcet, Borda, plurality, dictator) satisfy the Pareto condition on the unanimous profile.
Explain how \rho in the CES social welfare function connects to inequality aversion, via the two extremes \rho = 1 and \rho \to -\infty.
Explain why Arrow's theorem does not mean "democracy is impossible", via what the conditions (U, P, IIA, D) exactly rule out.
With \pi = 1/2, signal accuracy q = 0.7, R = 120, L = 80, compute the value of information \text{VoI}.
Let X \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 100] and search cost c = 12.5. Find the reservation value r^* and the expected number of searches under the optimal policy, and verify V(r^*) = r^* by direct computation.
Prove that the value of information is always zero when signal accuracy is q = 1/2. Verify with the numerical example \pi = 0.4, R = 100, L = 60.
From the reservation-policy value V(r) = \frac{M+r}{2} - \frac{cM}{M-r} and the indifference condition c = \frac{(M-r^*)^2}{2M}, prove algebraically that V(r^*) = r^*.
In the lemons market with m = 1.5, suppose the current price is p = 0.8. Find the average quality of the cars offered, the buyer's willingness to pay, and the next-step price p_1.

In the signaling model with \theta_H = 2, \theta_L = 1, c(e,\theta) = e/\theta, show that e^* = 2 is also a separating equilibrium, and compare the size of the waste with the least-cost equilibrium e^* = 1.
In the screening model with \theta_H = 2, \theta_L = 1, \lambda = 0.95, find the optimal menu, show that the low type is excluded from the market, and compute the welfare loss.
When m < 2, show that the unraveling map f(p) = mp/2 is a contraction on [0, 1], and use this to prove that the unraveling process converges to p^* = 0 from any starting price.

With p_1 = 0.8, p_0 = 0.2, \bar u = 20, u(w) = w^{1/2}, c = 10, the optimal contract (w_L, w_H) = (277.78, 1111.11) is given. Compute the agent's expected utility under high effort and the payoff from shirking, and show the incentive-compatibility constraint holds with equality.
Prove with Jensen's inequality that the risk premium C_1 - (\bar u + c)^{1/\alpha} is always nonnegative. When does equality hold? Check with the numerical example \alpha = 1/2, c = 10.

Let \alpha = 1/2, p_1 = 0.8, p_0 = 0.2, x_H = 2000, x_L = 0, \bar u = 20. If the effort cost is c = 25, should the principal implement high effort or settle for low effort? Answer by computing both profits directly.

Prove that the threshold effort cost c^* increases in the risk-aversion parameter \alpha: the less the agent dislikes risk, the more expensive an effort the principal is willing to incentivize. Verify by direct computation that c^* = 1200 when \alpha = 1.
In the one-buyer auction with v \sim U[0,1], compute expected revenue at reserves r = 0.2 and r = 0.8, and compare each with the optimal reserve's revenue.
With reserve r = 0.5, what is the payoff of a buyer with value v = 0.4 who reports \hat{v} = 0.8? Compare with truth-telling and confirm in this example that the gain from lying cannot exceed zero.
My value is v = 70 and the opponent bids truthfully. If I bid b = 50, what are my expected payoff and win probability? Find the loss relative to truthful bidding.

Consider a symmetric auction with two bidders whose values are i.i.d. U[0,1]. Using that the optimal mechanism "sells to the bidder with the highest virtual value, only when that virtual value is nonnegative", show the optimal reserve is still r^* = 0.5 and compute the expected revenue.

The base profile \theta is agent 1: c \succ a \succ b, agent 2: a \succ b \succ c. Under perturbation 1 (agent 2: a \succ c \succ b), compute f_{\text{anti}}(\theta) and f_{\text{anti}}(\theta'), and confirm that x = c fell for neither agent.

Under the dictatorial rule f_{\text{dict}}, look at perturbation 4 (agent 1: a \succ c \succ b). Show that x = f_{\text{dict}}(\theta) fell for agent 1, and explain why this is still not a monotonicity violation.
Explain at the level of ideas — not a formal proof — why a social choice rule implementable in Nash equilibrium must satisfy Maskin monotonicity. Use the whistle-blower intuition.

Suppose f is fully implemented in Nash equilibrium by a mechanism \Gamma = (M, g). Let x = f(\theta), and suppose moving to \theta' the outcome x fell for no agent. Show that a Nash equilibrium m^* at \theta remains a Nash equilibrium at \theta', and conclude f(\theta') = x.
